def.en: The load the ventricle pushes against during ejection, largely set by blood pressure and valve narrowing.
No wall thickening or motion in a segment during systole.
Wrap around of fast Doppler flow that the pulse rate cannot track, shown as colour reversal.
A permanent widening of a vessel to 30 mm or more in the abdominal aorta, or a weak bulging wall segment.
The fibrous ring where a valve leaflet hinges.
The great artery that carries oxygen rich blood from the left ventricle to the body.
The first part of the aorta holding the three cusps and the coronary origins.
The pointed tip of the left ventricle at the bottom of the apical views.
A false echo feature from physics or settings, not from anatomy.
An upper receiving chamber, right for body blood and left for lung blood.
The second inflow peak from atrial squeeze in late diastole.
A Doppler control that moves the zero line to show fast one way flow without wrap.
The rule that pressure drop in mmHg equals four times peak velocity squared.
An aortic valve with two cusps instead of three, prone to early stenosis.
Bright calcium deposits that stiffen cusps and shadow behind them.
Stroke volume times heart rate, the litres per minute the heart pumps.
Fine cords from papillary muscle tips to leaflet edges that stop prolapse.
A narrowing of the aortic isthmus that raises arm pressure above leg pressure.
Colour overlay showing flow direction and speed over the grey image.
Doppler that records all velocities along a line, best for high gradients.
The vein in the posterior groove draining heart muscle blood to the right atrium.
The time the early inflow wave takes to fall to zero, long in slow relaxation.
How far the sector looks; extra depth shrinks the heart and slows the frame rate.
The quiet mid diastolic pause between early filling and the atrial kick.
The relaxed filling half of the cycle after the T wave.
Enlargement of a chamber or vessel beyond its normal range.
A copy of a vessel painted by a strong reflector, moving exactly with the true one.
Blood splitting the aortic wall through a tear, with a flap dividing two lumens.
A false gap where an off axis beam misses a thin wall such as the septum.
A segment that bulges outward in systole instead of thickening.
The early diastolic speed of the mitral ring on tissue Doppler, low in slow relaxation.
The first inflow peak from early diastolic suction.
Timing echo frames and measurements to the ECG trace.
The true functional hole of a regurgitant or stenotic valve in sq cm.
The percent of diastolic volume ejected each beat, 55 percent or more being normal.
The frame at QRS start when the ventricle is fullest, used for size measurement.
The frame at aortic valve closure when the ventricle is emptiest.
A thin flap at the cava mouth that can mimic a mass or shunt flow.
The depth where the beam is narrowest and lateral detail is sharpest.
A cut that misses the true apex and flatters function while understating length.
The percent fall in right ventricular area each beat, 35 percent or more being normal.
The percent fall in cavity diameter each beat on M mode.
Images per second; high rates freeze fast valves and motion.
Probe frequency in MHz; high frequency suits children and near views, low suits adults.
Overall brightness; too much fills blood with noise and hides thrombus.
Imaging at twice the sent frequency for a cleaner picture with less clutter.
A liver vein draining to the cava whose Doppler pattern reports right heart pressure.
Thickened walls from pressure load or inherited muscle disease.
Reduced wall thickening in a segment during systole.
The entry path to a ventricle through its atrioventricular valve.
Left atrial volume divided by body surface area, normal below 34 ml per sq m.
A one line time trace showing motion such as valve opening through the cycle.
Mitral ring travel toward the apex each beat, a long axis function marker.
A normal muscle bar across the right ventricle, not thrombus.
The fastest speed pulsed Doppler can show before wrap, raised by a higher pulse rate.
The exit path from a ventricle to its great artery.
The ECG wave of atrial squeeze just before the QRS.
A cone of muscle anchoring the chordae inside the ventricle.
The window at the left sternal edge for long and short axis views.
A persisting foetal vessel between trunk and aorta with continuous flow.
Fluid in the sac around the heart, measured as diastolic echo free space.
The bright fibrous sac around the heart where fluid collects.
A flow convergence shell method for grading regurgitant orifice size.
The stretch on the ventricle before contraction, set by filling volume.
The time for a transmitral gradient to halve, used as 220 divided by area for mitral area.
The notch on the probe edge that always maps to one side of the screen.
A leaflet billowing back into the atrium in systole, sometimes with a leak.
Raised lung circulation pressure, read from tricuspid velocity plus atrial pressure.
Doppler that samples speed at one gate depth, best for timing and low velocities.
The ECG spike of ventricular activation that shuts the inflow valves.
Backward leak through a valve, graded by jet size, orifice and volume.
Repeating lines from a strong near reflector that can fake a flap.
Valve scarring after rheumatic fever, common in India, with fused commissures.
The small gate where pulsed Doppler listens.
The fan shaped ultrasound field spreading from the probe face.
A hole in the interatrial or interventricular wall with shunt flow on colour.
The wall between the ventricles or the atria.
A dark band behind calcium or rib where sound cannot pass.
Abnormal flow between chambers or vessels, such as through a defect or ductus.
Volume by stacked discs traced in two apical planes for ejection fraction.
Valve narrowing graded by velocity, gradient and area.
Millilitres pumped per beat, from outflow area times outflow velocity integral.
The window under the xiphoid looking up through the liver.
The window in the neck notch looking down at the arch.
The squeezing ejection half of the cycle between the sounds.
The ECG wave of ventricular recovery marking the end of systole.
Pressure from fluid that collapses chambers and needs urgent drainage.
Tricuspid ring travel toward the apex each beat, 17 mm or more being normal.
Clot, often apical after infarction, that sits still while walls move.
Doppler of muscle motion itself, used for ring speeds such as e prime.
Infected mass stuck on a leaflet that moves with it.
The narrow neck of a regurgitant jet, 7 mm or more marking severe tricuspid leak.
A lower pumping chamber, left to the body and right to the lungs.
A Doppler control that removes slow wall motion so slow flow can show.
